questions.question: What is stratigraphic context? / [CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• What is stratigraphic context?
  • Stratigraphic context refers to the position of artefacts, features, or deposits within
  • soil layers at an archaeological site. It helps archaeologists determine the
  • chronological sequence of human activities based on the principle that lower layers
  • are generally older than upper layers, ensuring accurate interpretation and dating of
  • archaeological remains.

questions.question: What is sample collection? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is sample collection?
  • Sample collection in archaeology is the systematic gathering of soil, charcoal, bones,
  • seeds, pottery, or other materials from excavation sites for scientific analysis. It helps
  • in dating, environmental reconstruction, dietary studies, and understanding past
  • human activities while ensuring accurate recording and preservation of
  • archaeological evidence for future research

questions.question: What are primary sources in archaeological research? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What are primary sources in archaeological research?
  • Primary sources in archaeological research are original materials directly related to
  • the past, such as artefacts, inscriptions, monuments, coins, pottery, manuscripts,
  • bones, and excavation records. They provide first-hand evidence about ancient
  • cultures, human activities, chronology, economy, religion, and social life, forming the
  • basic data for archaeological interpretation and analysis.

  • ensures accurate recording of depth, location, and spatial relationships throughout
  • the excavation process, helping maintain consistency and precision in archaeological
  • mapping, documentation, and interpretation of findings.

questions.question: How does probe survey reduce damage? / [CO2] [2x5 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• How does probe survey reduce damage?
  • A probe survey reduces damage by examining limited portions of an archaeological
  • site before large-scale excavation. It helps identify the presence, depth, and nature
  • of cultural remains with minimal disturbance. This method allows archaeologists to
  • plan excavation carefully, preserve important contexts, and avoid unnecessary
  • destruction of archaeological evidence and structures.

questions.question: Explain the methods of surface survey. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the methods of surface survey.
  • Surface survey in archaeology includes systematic walking, field observation,
  • collection of surface artefacts, aerial photography, satellite imagery, and GPS
  • mapping. Archaeologists identify pottery, tools, structures, and soil changes visible
  • on the ground surface. Transect survey and grid survey methods are commonly used
  • for accurate recording. Surface surveys help locate archaeological sites, understand
  • settlement patterns, and select areas for excavation with minimum disturbance to
  • cultural remains.

questions.question: Explain acoustic reflection principle. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain acoustic reflection principle
  • The acoustic reflection principle is a geophysical method in which sound waves are
  • transmitted into the ground or water and reflected back from buried objects, layers,
  • or structures. The returning echoes are recorded and analysed to identify subsurface
  • features. In archaeology, this principle is used in sonar and seismic surveys to detect
  • buried settlements, shipwrecks, walls, and geological formations without excavation.

questions.question: Discuss the importance of sieving. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the importance of sieving
  • Sieving is an important archaeological technique used to separate small artefacts
  • and ecofacts from excavated soil. It helps recover beads, bones, seeds, pottery
  • fragments, and tiny tools that may otherwise be missed during excavation. Sieving
  • improves accuracy in data collection, supports scientific analysis, and provides better
  • understanding of ancient diet, technology, environment, and cultural activities. It
  • also ensures maximum recovery of archaeological evidence from excavation
  • deposits.

questions.question: Discuss materials suitable for TL. / [CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss materials suitable for TL.
  • Thermoluminescence (TL) dating is mainly used for materials that were previously
  • heated at high temperatures. Suitable materials include pottery, terracotta, bricks,
  • burnt stones, hearths, kiln remains, and fired clay objects. Certain minerals such as
  • quartz and feldspar are also used. TL dating measures trapped electrons released
  • during reheating and helps determine the time elapsed since the material was last
  • heated. It is useful for dating prehistoric and ancient cultural remains.

questions.question: Describe landscape archaeology. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe landscape archaeology.
  • Landscape archaeology is the study of the relationship between human activities and
  • the natural environment over time. It examines settlements, roads, fields, water
  • systems, monuments, and ecological features within a wider geographical area.
  • Using surveys, GIS, aerial photography, and environmental analysis, archaeologists
  • understand how ancient people modified and interacted with landscapes. This
  • approach helps reconstruct patterns of settlement, economy, communication,
  • agriculture, and cultural development across different historical periods
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Describe the process of digital map preparation. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the process of digital map preparation
  • Digital map preparation involves collecting spatial data through surveys, GPS,
  • satellite imagery, aerial photographs, or excavation records. The data are entered
  • into computer software such as GIS for digitisation, layering, scaling, and analysis.
  • Features like contours, structures, roads, and archaeological sites are accurately
  • plotted. Symbols, legends, coordinates, and north arrows are added for clarity.
  • Digital maps improve accuracy, storage, updating, interpretation, and presentation
  • of archaeological and geographical information for research and planning purposes.

  • A magnetometer is a geophysical instrument used to measure variations in the
  • earth’s magnetic field caused by buried archaeological features. Objects such as
  • hearths, walls, pits, ditches, and fired structures create magnetic anomalies. The
  • instrument detects and records these changes while surveying the ground surface.
  • The collected data are converted into maps showing subsurface features.
  • Magnetometer surveys are non-destructive, rapid, and useful for locating hidden
  • archaeological remains without excavation or physical disturbance to the site.

questions.question: Describe the principles of stratigraphy and the use of Harris Matrix in archaeological interpretation / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the principles of stratigraphy and the use of Harris Matrix in archaeological
  • interpretation
  • Stratigraphy is the study of soil layers or strata in archaeological excavation to
  • understand the chronological sequence of human activities. It is based on the
  • principle of superposition, which states that lower layers are generally older than
  • upper layers. Other principles include original horizontality, association, and
  • stratigraphic succession. Each layer, feature, or deposit represents a separate
  • archaeological context that helps reconstruct past events and occupation phases.
  • The Harris Matrix, developed by Edward Cecil Harris, is a diagrammatic system used
  • to record and interpret stratigraphic relationships between archaeological contexts.
  • It arranges layers and features in chronological order, showing which deposits came
  • earlier or later. The Harris Matrix helps archaeologists organise excavation data
  • systematically, identify site formation processes, and reconstruct cultural sequences
  • accurately. It is widely used in modern archaeology for excavation recording,
  • analysis, and interpretation of complex archaeological sites.

questions.question: Discuss applications of K-Ar dating method in archaeology / [CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss applications of K-Ar dating method in archaeology
  • Potassium–Argon (K–Ar) dating is an absolute dating method used to determine the
  • age of volcanic rocks and ash layers associated with archaeological and prehistoric
  • remains. It is based on the radioactive decay of potassium-40 into argon-40 over
  • long periods of time. This method is especially useful for dating very ancient sites
  • beyond the range of radiocarbon dating.
  • K–Ar dating is widely applied in prehistoric archaeology, palaeoanthropology, and
  • geological studies. It helps establish the age of early human fossils, stone tools, and
  • volcanic deposits associated with hominid activities. Important prehistoric sites in
  • East Africa, such as Olduvai Gorge, have been dated using this method. It also assists
  • archaeologists in constructing chronological frameworks for human evolution and
  • cultural development. Since volcanic materials are common in many archaeological
  • regions, K–Ar dating provides reliable and scientifically accurate dates for ancient
  • archaeological contexts, particularly those older than several hundred thousand
  • years.

questions.question: Evaluate limitations of relative dating methods. / [CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate limitations of relative dating methods.
  • Relative dating methods determine the chronological sequence of archaeological
  • materials without providing exact calendar dates. One major limitation is that they
  • only establish whether an object or layer is older or younger than another. Methods
  • such as stratigraphy and typology depend heavily on undisturbed contexts; natural
  • disturbances, erosion, animal activity, or human interference may alter original
  • layers and produce inaccurate interpretations.
  • Relative dating is also influenced by regional cultural variations, making comparison
  • between different sites difficult. Typological dating may become unreliable when
  • artefact styles continue for long periods or are reused by later cultures. These
  • methods cannot independently determine the absolute age of archaeological
  • remains and often require support from scientific dating techniques such as
  • radiocarbon or thermoluminescence dating. In addition, incomplete excavation
  • records and lack of associated materials may reduce reliability. Therefore, although
  • relative dating is fundamental in archaeology, its limitations make it necessary to
  • combine it with absolute dating methods for accurate chronological interpretation.

questions.question: Explain the structure and components of a standard excavation report. / [CO1] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the structure and components of a standard excavation report.
  • A standard excavation report is a systematic record of archaeological excavation and
  • findings. It generally begins with an introduction explaining the site location,
  • objectives, historical background, and significance of the excavation. This is followed
  • by methodology, describing survey methods, excavation techniques, sampling
  • procedures, recording systems, and scientific analyses used during the investigation.
  • The main body contains detailed descriptions of stratigraphy, trenches, layers,
  • structures, artefacts, ecofacts, and features discovered during excavation. Plans, maps,
  • photographs, section drawings, and tables are included for accurate documentation.
  • Interpretation and analysis explain cultural sequences, chronology, settlement
  • patterns, economy, religion, and other aspect of past human activity.
  • The report concludes with findings, conclusions, and recommendations for future
  • research or conservation. Bibliography, appendices, catalogues, and excavation
  • registers are also important components. A properly prepared excavation report
  • ensures scientific accuracy, preservation of archaeological data, and future reference
  • for researchers and heritage management.
